VAN BUILD / ELECTRICAL / DONE AND DUSTED

A battery monitor for my van’s power station.

My van runs on an EcoFlow River 2 Pro. To see how much battery is left, you look at the unit itself or open the phone app. I wanted a small screen that is always there, so I built one.

Get the code on GitHub ↗
Works with
River 2 / 2 Max / 2 Pro
Parts
One board, one USB cable
Wiring
None
Build time
About 30 minutes
01 / THE PROBLEM

Why a power station needs its own monitor.

A portable power station is the simplest way to put electricity in a camper van. Battery, inverter, solar charge controller and 12V socket in one box. Nothing to wire, nothing to fuse.

Mine sits above the wheel well, under the bed. So this monitor is mostly about convenience. I don’t want to crawl under there every time I need to check the charge or switch an outlet.

The battery already measures its own charge and power. It sends those numbers to the EcoFlow app over Bluetooth. This project is a small screen that listens to the same numbers, so they are on display all the time.

02 / WHAT IT DOES

The numbers that matter, and two switches.

  • Battery percentage, to one decimal place.
  • Watts in and watts out, so you can see what solar is delivering and what the fridge is pulling.
  • Time left, or time to full while it is charging.
  • AC and 12V buttons that switch the outlets and the car socket on and off. Each button changes colour only once the battery confirms it has switched.
  • Screen sleep. The backlight goes dark after a minute so it doesn’t shine in my face at night. It wakes up with a tap.
  • Reconnects by itself after the battery is switched off or goes out of range.
  • No phone, no Wi-Fi, no cloud. It works in a campsite with no signal.
03 / THE PARTS

One board. One cable.

  • ESP32-2432S028R, better known as the Cheap Yellow Display. It is an ESP32 with Bluetooth, a 2.8-inch touchscreen and a USB port, on one board that arrives fully built.
04 / HOW IT WORKS

It talks to the battery the way the app does.

The River 2 series advertises itself over Bluetooth LE. The board finds it, does the same encrypted handshake the EcoFlow app does, and proves it belongs to you with your EcoFlow account’s user id. After that the battery sends a status update every few seconds, and the board draws it.

I didn’t reverse-engineer the protocol myself. It is ported to C++ from rabits/ha-ef-ble, the Home Assistant integration that worked it out.
